clue.text: Small airline for part of Russia

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
Iberia is the Spanish national airline

explanation.surface: Someone looking for a little regional carrier to fly them somewhere in Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'small airline' as one idea, but 'Small' is just its abbreviation and the airline is the Spanish flag carrier.
explanation.definitionFit: Siberia is the vast northern Asian region that makes up most of the Russian landmass.

blocks.note: a sack is a large bag
'but' can mean only, as in 'she is but a child'

explanation.surface: A musical instrument that needs nothing more than a bag, like bagpipes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Only' looks like a qualifier on the bag, but it supplies the archaic word meaning merely.
explanation.definitionFit: The sackbut is an early form of trombone played in Renaissance and Baroque music.

clue.text: Possibly scarf fruit eating rind’s end

indicators.note: an end is the final point, so only the last letter of the word is kept
whatever eats something takes it inside, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: a common yellow fruit
the closing letter of the word rind

explanation.surface: Someone scoffing a piece of fruit, right down to the end of the peel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scarf' tempts as the verb to eat greedily, which fits the eating surface, but here it is the neckwear noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A bandana is a large coloured handkerchief worn around the head or neck, one kind of scarf, hence 'possibly'.

clue.text: Rises in opposition to something, initially

definitions.text: Rises in opposition to something, initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so the opening letter of each word is taken

blocks.note: the opening letters of these five words

explanation.surface: A description of people rising up against something they object to.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: its first letters spell the answer, and the complete clue also describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Riots are violent public disturbances, typically uprisings by crowds protesting against authority or a grievance.

clue.text: Nice beer, a lager, almost drunk

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the final letter is dropped
someone drunk staggers about in disorder, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the word lager without its last letter

explanation.surface: A drinker praising a beer, having nearly finished the lager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' looks like the drinker's verdict on the beer, but it is the definition; 'drunk' works on the letters rather than the drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something pleasant and enjoyable, so they are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Stick with recording equipment for debate

blocks.note: a pole is a long stick
MIC is short for microphone

explanation.surface: A boom microphone on a pole, set up to capture a public debate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' reads as a verb, stick with, but it is the noun for a rod.
explanation.definitionFit: A polemic is a strongly argued attack on an opinion, the kind of contentious argument found in controversy.

clue.text: Bit of silence for the audience

indicators.note: an audience listens, so the word is heard rather than read

blocks.note: peace means quiet or silence

explanation.surface: A request for a moment's hush from the people in the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words are pronounced identically; the quiet one is spelt with EA.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece and a bit both mean a small portion or fragment of something larger.

clue.text: Pass law and member falls behind?

blocks.note: a leg is a limb, a member of the body
someone who falls behind is late, read as two words IS LATE

explanation.surface: Parliament passes a law while one of its members lags behind the vote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests a Member of Parliament in the lawmaking scene; it is a body part, and the question mark flags the loose phrase for being late.
explanation.definitionFit: To legislate is to make or enact laws, which is what a parliament does when it passes them.

clue.text: Waspish matron bustling about ward, finally

indicators.note: bustling means moving busily in all directions, so the letters are rearranged
about means around, so one part goes round another
finally means at the end, so only the last letter is taken

blocks.note: taken as written, before rearranging
the closing letter of the word ward

explanation.surface: A sharp-tongued hospital matron hurrying around a ward at the end of her shift.
explanation.walkthrough: The matron's letters are rearranged and wrapped around the last letter of the hospital room. A matron is the senior nurse in a British hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: Waspish and mordant both describe sharp, biting, sarcastic speech or humour that stings.

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
a radiator is a heater

explanation.surface: Someone tinkering with a radiator that has gone cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddles' suggests fiddling with the knobs; here it means swindles.
explanation.definitionFit: To fiddle is slang for cheating or swindling, so a person who fiddles is a cheat.

blocks.note: a con is a convict
a spell or tour is a period of duty, as in a tour of duty

explanation.surface: The appearance of a prisoner about to serve a stretch in jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spell' looks like a prison sentence or magic, but it is a stint of duty.
explanation.definitionFit: A contour is an outline or shape, the form of something traced along its edge.

clue.text: Fill bare menu with Cheddar, say

indicators.note: something bare is stripped, so the outer letters are removed leaving the middle

blocks.note: the inner two letters of menu
Cheddar Gorge is a famous limestone ravine in Somerset, England

explanation.surface: Padding out a sparse menu by adding cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheddar looks like the cheese but is the Somerset village famous for its gorge; 'say' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: To engorge is to swell or fill to excess, typically with blood or liquid.

blocks.note: brassy means bold or impudent, so more brassy is saucier
the heart of the word sweet is its middle letter

explanation.surface: A cheeky girlfriend flashing a bit of her lingerie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweetheart' reads as a lover but is split as the heart, or central letter, of sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: A brassiere, or bra, is a woman's undergarment supporting the breasts, one item of underwear.

indicators.note: to pursue is to chase behind, so this piece is placed after the other

blocks.note: to scan is to study closely
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Too short a period left over to continue one's studies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little time' reads as one phrase, but 'Little' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Scant means barely sufficient or small in amount, so it describes a little of something.

blocks.note: in Yorkshire dialect 'the' is clipped to t'
a rail is a bar

explanation.surface: A dog lying about in a pub in the north of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog' is a verb, to follow closely. Yorkshire speech famously shortens 'the' to t', as in 'down t'pub'.
explanation.definitionFit: To dog someone and to trail them both mean to follow persistently behind them.

indicators.note: set free, the letters are loosed from their order and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, before rearranging

explanation.surface: An excited punter anticipating complimentary lap dances at a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prospect' looks like a hope or chance, but here it is a view.
explanation.definitionFit: A prospect is an extensive view over countryside, which is what a landscape is.

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: better means improved
a spa is a health resort

explanation.surface: Someone feeling better after a spa visit with its showers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shower' is a verb, to spray or splash, not a noun in a bathroom.
explanation.definitionFit: To bespatter is to splash all over with drops of liquid or dirt, as a shower would.

blocks.note: someone planted in a chair is seated
irises are flowers

explanation.surface: Men perhaps putting flowers in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guys' reads as men but is the verb to guy, to mock or ridicule; 'maybe' marks the loose equivalence.
explanation.definitionFit: To guy someone is to make fun of them, and satirising is a form of mockery through ridicule.

clue.text: Subject of French writer with depression

blocks.note: de is French for of
a pen is a writing implement
a dent is a small depression in a surface

explanation.surface: The theme of a melancholy French novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subject' seems to be a topic, and 'depression' low mood; both are other senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Being subject to someone means being under their control, reliant on them, as a dependent person is.

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a deed is an action
BA is Bachelor of Arts, made plural

explanation.surface: Single men up to no good and getting into seedy behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bachelors' suggests single men, but here it means graduates holding BA degrees.
explanation.definitionFit: Debased means morally degraded or corrupted, close in sense to sordid or vile.

indicators.note: something shot is ruined or broken, so the letters are knocked out of order
to contain is to hold within, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: taken as written, before rearranging
P is the abbreviation for power in physics

explanation.surface: A science-fiction ray gun possibly fired at full power.
explanation.walkthrough: A phaser is the ray gun from Star Trek; 'shot' suggests firing it but signals rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words express uncertainty or possibility, so they are ordinary synonyms.

blocks.note: an ex is a former spouse or partner
first is written 1st, with the 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: Moving back in with an old flame before anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' looks like a position instruction, but it gives letters: the ordinal 1ST with the digit read as I.
explanation.definitionFit: To live and to exist both mean to be alive or have being.

clue.text: Run over, steaming round empty thoroughfare

indicators.note: emptied of its contents, a word keeps only its outer letters
going round something means surrounding it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: steaming means furiously angry
the first and last letters of thoroughfare

explanation.surface: A furious driver after being run over on a deserted road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run over' tempts as a road accident; it means to repeat or go over again.
explanation.definitionFit: To iterate is to repeat or restate, and to run over something is to go through it again.

clue.text: Muscle runs enclosing ends of clavicle

indicators.note: the ends of a word are its outermost letters, first and last
to enclose is to surround, so one piece is placed inside another

blocks.note: trips and runs are both short journeys
the first and last letters of clavicle

explanation.surface: An anatomy note about a muscle that stretches to the collarbone.
explanation.walkthrough: The anatomical surface hides that 'runs' means excursions, not a muscle running from bone to bone.
explanation.definitionFit: The triceps is the large three-headed muscle at the back of the upper arm.

clue.text: Crows perhaps in efforts surrounding rook

indicators.note: surrounding means placed all around, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: a bid is an attempt or effort
R is the chess notation for rook

explanation.surface: Crows making attempts to mob a rook, another member of their family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rook' fits the bird scene but is the chess piece, abbreviated as in notation.
explanation.definitionFit: Crows are one example of the feathered creatures, hence 'perhaps' marking an instance.

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild and are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, before rearranging
taken as written, before rearranging

explanation.surface: A simple plot of land growing unripe bananas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green bananas' reads as unripe fruit; 'Plain' reads as an adjective, but it is the grassland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Serengeti is a vast grassland plain in Tanzania, famous for wildlife migration.

indicators.note: some means a portion, so only part of the running text is used

blocks.note: the letters run across the word break

explanation.surface: A tasting note on a glass of sharp-flavoured schnapps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' looks like the drink, matching schnapps, but it is an evil spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: Satan is the Devil, the chief evil spirit in Christian and Jewish tradition.

indicators.note: a received signal is picked up by ear, so the word is heard

blocks.note: to knead is to massage by pressing and working

explanation.surface: Someone longing for the massages they are given.
explanation.walkthrough: The silent K means the two words sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: To yearn for something is to long for or require it, which is what one needs.

clue.text: Marine worker holding line for caulk?

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: marine means of the sea
a worker ant; 'worker' is a crossword staple for ANT or BEE
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A sailor holding a line, ready to caulk a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marine worker' suggests a sailor or soldier, but it splits into the sea and an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: Caulk is a waterproof filler for seams, one kind of substance used to seal gaps, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Returning, say, adult makes water leak

indicators.note: returning means going back the way you came, so the order is turned back to front

blocks.note: e.g. means for example, as does say
A is the abbreviation for adult, as in film ratings
to make water is to urinate

explanation.surface: A grown-up on the way back relieving themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Makes water leak' reads as causing a leak, but 'makes water' is a euphemism and 'leak' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Seepage is liquid slowly escaping through a porous material or small opening, just as in a leak.

indicators.note: including something means taking it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a disc is a gramophone record
N is the abbreviation for name
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: A record label naming a spot that features the band Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot' reads as a place or a stain, but it is the verb to notice.
explanation.definitionFit: To spot something is to notice or perceive it, and discern means to perceive or detect.

indicators.note: to constrain is to hold in, so the letters sit enclosed in the running text

blocks.note: the letters run across three words

explanation.surface: A curt abbess keeping her nuns on a short leash.
explanation.walkthrough: The abbess and nuns form one convent scene, and the answer sits in the words describing her.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuns are addressed as Sister, the title for members of a female religious order.
